# Modeling

Three problems, one shared pipeline:

| Problem | Type | Models |
|---|---|---|
| 1. KPI forecasting | Time series / regression | Seasonal naive, Holt-Winters, linear, random forest, gradient boosting |
| 2. Data-quality anomalies | Anomaly detection | Z-score rule (\|z\| > 4) |
| 3. SLA drivers | Regression + importance | Gradient boosting, permutation importance |

## Forecasting — time-based split, no leakage

```{r forecast}
pipe <- run_pipeline("../data/synthetic", "../data/processed")
bf <- build_features(pipe$daily, "sla_attainment_pct",
                     include_operational = FALSE)
sp <- time_split(bf$frame, test_days = 61)
ml <- train_ml_forecasters(sp$train[, bf$features, drop = FALSE],
                           sp$train$sla_attainment_pct)
preds <- predict_ml(ml, sp$test[, bf$features, drop = FALSE])
regression_metrics(sp$test$sla_attainment_pct, preds$gbm)
```

## Holt-Winters (base R `stats::HoltWinters`)

```{r hw}
hw <- holt_winters_forecast(sp$train$sla_attainment_pct, steps = 14)
hw$forecast
```

## Anomaly detection

```{r anomaly}
hf <- anomaly_features(pipe$health)
det <- detect_anomalies(hf, ANOMALY_FEATURES)
anomaly_metrics(hf$is_anomaly, det$flag)
```

## Why gradient boosting wins here

The SLA series is driven by interacting operational levers
(staffing ratio × backlog pressure), which a linear model can only
approximate additively. Gradient boosting captures the interaction
without sacrificing interpretability — permutation importance still
tells the stakeholder which lever matters.
